name: Esther Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther, I'm 27, and I live with my partner Tomás in a rented flat about twenty minutes from the depot. He drives the number 9 bus, so between his early starts and my nights we mostly meet over breakfast. I left school at fifteen and did shop work and cleaning before I got into the warehouse three years ago. It pays better than anything I've done, and I've been careful with it, so I've got a decent bit put away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights in the chilled section of a big supermarket distribution centre, ten at night to six in the morning. I get my pick list on the scanner gun, push a pallet truck round the aisles, and build cages of yoghurts, milk and ready meals for the stores. The cold gets into your hands even with gloves, and I'm still slower than most, about 140 cases an hour when the target is 160. What I like is the crew, the quiet at three in the morning and the fact the night pay is properly good. What wears me out is the rate screen telling me I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most days already. Every year someone in a suit walks round with a new screen and says it'll change everything, and then we're still pushing pallets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the canteen: told you so. The bosses talk about AI like it's magic, but the milk still needs lifting. Online I don't post much, but I'd probably share something from the union saying the hype was about squeezing us, not helping us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, because I don't want to learn some new system at my age with my reading. The rate screen and the scanner are already enough for me. If nothing big changes, I keep my nights, my night premium and my savings keep growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my shifts and keep putting my overtime money into my savings account, like I've done since I started. I'd keep going to the union meetings once a month at the community hall. And I'd still try to get my pick rate up, because that's the thing that could actually get me in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the world I already know, and I'm good at living in it. The only thing nagging me is the rate, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said routine tasks get automated a bit. Is there anything in your shift that could go, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the bit where the team leader prints the labels and sorts out the shorts, when a store's order is missing stock. A computer could do that, and it already half does. That's Karen's job, my team leader, not mine. My job is the cold and the lifting, and nobody's building a cheap machine for that in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money you keep saving, if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás and I want a deposit for a flat of our own, something with a balcony. We've got about nine months of bills saved between my account and a bit my nan left me. I'd just keep adding to that and not touch it. I don't buy shares or anything like that, I don't trust it.

say: I'd tell the canteen the **AI hype** was mostly bosses talking, and the **milk** still needs lifting.
I'd share a **union post** saying the hype was about squeezing workers, not helping them.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because learning a new system with my reading is hard.
My **night premium** and steady shifts would carry on, so my **savings** keep growing.
do: Keep working **nights** in chilled and put **overtime money** into savings every month.
Go to the monthly **union meeting** at the community hall, as I do now.
Work on getting my **pick rate** up from 140 towards the target of 160.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the world I already know how to live in.
A small **nag** about my pick rate, which is a bigger worry than robots.
S0.quote: My job is the cold and the lifting, and nobody's building a cheap machine for that in this picture.
fieldNote: Her real worry is the **rate screen**, not AI; being slow is her daily pressure.
Strong **savings** and a partner on steady bus wages make this scenario feel secure.
She separates her job from her **team leader's** paperwork, which she sees as the automatable part.

steps.text: Keep working night shifts in the chilled section
Put overtime pay into the flat deposit savings each month
Attend the monthly union meeting at the community hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so this one's more real. I can already see bits of it, like the new system that tells the trucks when to come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say: watch the office, not us, because that's where it hits first. With friends I'd say the company will use it as an excuse to push the rates up again. I'd be loud about it at union meetings, because that's where it counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my own hands-on job is safe for a while, but the people around me change. Karen's job shrinks, the planners go, and the new software decides how many of us are needed each night. That's the bit that scares me, a computer setting the rota and the targets with nobody to argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get something in writing about how the new software sets our targets, this year, before it's switched on. I'd keep saving, maybe even more, and I'd ask Tomás if we can wait on the flat for a year. I wouldn't go learning AI stuff myself, I'd leave that to the young ones on days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own pay looks fine for now, but the ground's moving under everyone around me. I don't like it when things move and I can't see where.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave AI to the young ones. You're 27. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, fair. I'm young on paper but I feel old with phones and screens. I never finished school and reading long instructions makes me panic a bit. I'd rather be good at the thing I do than bad at a new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karen, honestly, and the two women in the transport office who book the lorries. They've been there fifteen years and their whole job is planning and phoning. I'd worry they get told to come down on the floor with us, at our pay, and they've got bad backs.

say: I'd say at work that the **office jobs** get hit first, not the pickers on the floor.
I'd warn friends the company will use **new software** as an excuse to push **pick rates** up.
think: My own **hands-on job** looks safe for a while, but the people around me change.
Software setting the **rota and targets**, with nobody to argue with, is what really scares me.
do: Push the **union** this year for a written deal on how software sets **targets**.
Keep **saving** and ask Tomás to wait a year on buying the **flat**.
Skip **AI courses** and focus on getting better at picking.
feel: **Uneasy**, because her own pay looks fine but everything around her is moving.
Worried for **older colleagues** in the office whose planning work disappears.
S1.quote: I'd rather be good at the thing I do than bad at a new thing.
fieldNote: She fears software as a **boss** more than as a replacement; targets set by a machine.
Her answer is **collective**: get rules in writing through the union rather than retrain.
She calls herself **old with screens** at 27, a clear sign of her resistance to change.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to negotiate written rules on software-set targets
Hold off on the flat purchase for one more year
Raise monthly savings from overtime by another shift's pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before Tomás and I would even have the flat. And then robots three years after that, so 2031 for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed, and I'd mean it. I'd sign every petition and go on every march the union organised. At work I'd tell people to join the union now, while we still have bodies on the floor that the company needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm out of a job by 2031 and I don't know what I'd do instead. My job is the lifting and the walking, which buys me three years, but after that a robot that doesn't feel the cold will do my shift. I left school at fifteen, so I'm not the one who gets the new jobs looking after the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything extra and push my savings as far as I could, maybe a year and a half of bills. I'd get more involved in the union, maybe as a rep, because I'd want to fight for redundancy pay and retraining money. I'd also vote for whoever promised to tax the companies using robots. I'd keep doing my shifts every single night until they told me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like seeing a lorry coming and you can't move out of the way. Some nights I'd lie awake thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with the flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's off. You don't sign a mortgage when you think your job's gone in five years. Tomás's job is driving, and I'd guess driverless buses come too, so it's both of us. We'd keep renting and keep the money in the bank where we can reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're slow to learn new things. Is there anything, in those three years, you'd be willing to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a forklift licence, because it's still the floor and the people I know. But I'd be learning to drive the thing the robot replaces next. Honestly, I'd rather put my energy into the union than into a course I'd probably fail.

say: I'd say AGI must be **slowed or stopped**, and I'd join every **union** march.
I'd tell everyone on the floor to **join the union now**, while the company still needs us.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2031, once robots can do my shift.
Leaving school at fifteen means I won't get the new **robot jobs**, and Tomás's driving looks **at risk** too.
do: Cut all extra spending and build savings towards a **year and a half** of bills.
Stand as a **union rep** to fight for redundancy pay and retraining money.
Vote for whoever promises to **tax companies** that use robots.
feel: **Alarmed**, like seeing a lorry coming with no way to move out of it.
Lying **awake at night** thinking about both incomes going.
S2.quote: I left school at fifteen, so I'm not the one who gets the new jobs looking after the robots.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** for robots doesn't comfort her; she reads it as a countdown.
Both household incomes feel **exposed**, since her partner drives a bus.
She turns fear into **collective action** rather than learning, consistent with her resistance.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and extras to grow savings to eighteen months of bills
Stand as union rep to fight for redundancy and retraining pay
Vote for parties that promise a tax on robot-using companies
Drop the flat purchase and keep renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so 2031 for the thinking stuff and 2034 for robots. That's eight years for my kind of job. It still lands while I'm young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that the companies need to share what they save with the workers. But I'd say it a bit less angrily, because there's time to get rules in place. I'd tell the younger ones on the floor to use the time and not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd think eight years is long enough to save properly and short enough that it's still my career that ends. I'd be 35 when the robots come. That's young enough to start over but I'd be starting with nothing on paper, no exams, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This first year I'd keep saving and get more active in the union, maybe start going to the regional meetings. I'd probably finally do the forklift licence, which the company pays for, so I'm worth a bit more in the meantime. And Tomás and I might buy the flat after all, a small one, because eight years is a lot of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lying-awake anxious. It's more like a deadline at the back of my head. I'd have some control, which I didn't feel in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're more willing to do the forklift licence here than in the fast picture. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in this one it actually pays off for a few years. In the fast one, a forklift licence felt like learning to ride a horse the year cars come in. With eight years, the extra pay adds up and it might help me get into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union fight for, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Notice periods, real ones, like a year's warning before a shift is automated. Retraining paid by the company, not some online course you do at midnight. And first refusal on any new jobs, like robot minders, for the people already there.

say: I'd say companies must **share the savings** with workers, but with time for **proper** rules.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **use the time** instead of waiting for the company.
think: Eight years is long enough to **save properly** but still ends my **career** young.
At **35**, I'd be starting again with **no exams** and nothing on paper.
do: Join the **regional union meetings** and push for a year's **notice** before automation.
Take the **forklift licence** the company pays for, to earn a bit more meanwhile.
Consider buying a **small flat** with Tomás, since eight years covers many **mortgage payments**.
feel: **Anxious**, but like a deadline at the back of her head, not sleepless.
A sense of **some control** that she lacked in the fast picture.
S3.quote: In the fast one, a forklift licence felt like learning to ride a horse the year cars come in.
fieldNote: Extra time unlocks **small personal steps**, like the forklift licence, she refused before.
Her union demands get **concrete**: notice periods, paid retraining, first refusal.
She still expects her **career to end** in her mid-thirties; the time only softens the blow.

steps.text: Attend regional union meetings to push for a year's automation notice
Take the company-paid forklift licence course this year
Keep saving overtime pay towards a smaller flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the thinking, then 2039 for robots. I'd be nearly 40 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when we need the government to plan properly, with a decade there's no excuse. I'd post union stuff about it, about making sure workers get a say. At work I'd probably joke that I'll be retired from the cold before the robots get here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I've got time but I'd still expect to lose this job eventually. Twelve years is a long time on nights, and maybe I'd want out of the cold by then anyway. What bothers me is not knowing what job there'd be to go to, for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Tomás, probably within two years, and keep saving on top. I'd do the forklift licence and maybe move to days. I'd stay active in the union, because ten years is enough to win real protections if enough of us push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still a bit anxious, because I know where it ends. But it's more like the way you think about getting old. It's coming, you can't stop it, so you plan a bit and live your life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might want out of the cold anyway. What would you want instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something warm, honestly. Maybe working in a school kitchen or a care home, something with people. But they'd want qualifications. Going back to class scares me more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to class, with ten years to do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one evening a week, if a friend did it with me. My friend Rosa from the chilled crew keeps talking about doing English and maths at the college. If she went, I'd go. On my own, I'd find excuses.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves the **government** no excuse not to plan properly.
I'd joke at work that I'll **retire from the cold** before the robots arrive.
think: I'd still expect to **lose this job** eventually, even with twelve years to go.
Not knowing what **job there'd be** for someone without exams bothers me most.
do: Buy a **flat** with Tomás within **two years** and keep saving on top.
Do the **forklift licence** and try to move to **day shifts**.
Stay active in the **union** to win protections over the decade.
feel: A **steady anxiety**, like thinking about getting old: coming, but plannable.
**Scared of the classroom** more than of the robots themselves.
S4.quote: Going back to class scares me more than robots.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **buy the flat**, a big shift from the fast picture.
Her real block is **school**: fear of the classroom, not of technology.
She'd only study if a **friend** came too, a useful lever for support.

steps.text: Buy a small flat with Tomás within two years
Take English and maths evening classes if Rosa signs up too
Keep pushing the union for long-term automation protections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. Five years to the robots and both of us, me and Tomás, in jobs a machine could take. What would help is real notice, a year at least, and the company paying for training that's in a classroom with people, not on a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being slow. Everyone talks about robots, but right now the thing that could get me sacked is a number on a screen saying I'm behind. I'd like someone to ask whether those targets are fair before they give them to a robot to set.

headlineQuote: Right now the thing that could get me sacked is a number on a screen saying I'm behind.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old night picker** in a supermarket's chilled warehouse, living with Tomás, a bus driver.
She left school at fifteen, is **slow with screens**, and never uses AI tools.
She has about **nine months saved** and a strong belief in the **union** as her protection.
She is calm if AI fizzles, but **alarmed** by AGI in two years, expecting both household jobs to go.
More time makes her **buy the flat** and try a forklift licence, yet classrooms scare her most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her picking job and Tomás's bus driving could both go within five years.
whatWouldHelp: At least a **year's notice** before jobs are automated.
Company-paid training in a **real classroom** with people, not on a screen.
